claim: The C. elegans pharynx contains 20 synaptically interconnected neurons that fall into 14 anatomically distinct classes.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans contains an autonomously acting nervous system in its foregut, the pharynx, composed of 20 synaptically interconnected neurons that fall into 14 anatomically distinct classes (Albertson and Thomson, 1976; Cook et al., 2020; Mango, 2007; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Albertson and Thomson, 1976; Cook et al., 2020; Mango, 2007) and reference to Figure 1 in the manuscript.

claim: The pharyngeal nervous system of C. elegans can be considered the enteric nervous system of C. elegans due to its association with the digestive tract.
source: Due to its association with the digestive tract of the worm, the pharyngeal nervous system can be considered to be the enteric nervous system of C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on the anatomical association of the pharyngeal nervous system with the digestive tract, which is an inference from established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The pharyngeal nervous system is required for movement of food through the digestive tract of the worm.
source: It is required for movement of food through the digestive tract of the worm and functions in an entirely autonomous manner, even if removed from the rest of the animal (Albertson and Thomson, 1976; Avery, 2012; Cook et al., 2020; Mango, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature describing the function of the pharyngeal nervous system.

claim: The pharyngeal nervous system functions in an entirely autonomous manner, even if removed from the rest of the animal.
source: It is required for movement of food through the digestive tract of the worm and functions in an entirely autonomous manner, even if removed from the rest of the animal (Albertson and Thomson, 1976; Avery, 2012; Cook et al., 2020; Mango, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature describing the autonomous function of the pharyngeal nervous system.

claim: The pharyngeal nervous system is connected to the remainder of the nervous system through a single nerve fiber, that of the bilateral RIP neuron pair.
source: Like other enteric nervous systems, the nematode pharyngeal nervous system constitutes a non-centralized neuronal network isolated from the rest of the nervous system and, in rough analogy to the vagus nerve, is connected to the remainder of the nervous system through a single nerve fiber, that of the bilateral RIP neuron pair (Albertson and Thomson, 1976; Cook et al., 2020; Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature describing the connectivity of the pharyngeal nervous system.

claim: Pharyngeal neurons have sensory, inter- and motorneuron function.
source: Like vertebrate enteric neurons (Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020), pharyngeal neurons have sensory, inter- and motorneuron function (Avery and Horvitz, 1989; Cook et al., 2020; Trojanowski et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the functional properties of pharyngeal neurons.

claim: Most pharyngeal neurons each combine sensory, inter- and motorneuron function, that is, are polymodal.
source: Our recent re-analysis of pharyngeal nervous system anatomy has shown that rather than segregating these functions over distinct neurons as vertebrates do (Fung and Vanden Berghe, 2020), most pharyngeal neurons each combine sensory, inter- and motorneuron function, that is, are polymodal (Cook et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Cook et al., 2020) describing the polymodal nature of pharyngeal neurons.

claim: The 14 distinct pharyngeal neuron types are defined by their unique anatomy, that is, axonal projections, morphology, synaptic connectivity.
source: The 14 distinct pharyngeal neuron types are defined by their unique anatomy, that is, axonal projections, morphology, synaptic connectivity (Figure 1B and C; Cook et al., 2020), and unique functional features (Avery and Horvitz, 1989; Trojanowski et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and reference to Figure 1B and C showing anatomical features.

claim: Each pharyngeal neuron class is uniquely defined by characteristic signatures of neurotransmitter systems, from acetylcholine (ACh), glutamate (Glu) to serotonin, and by unique combinations of neuropeptide-encoding genes.
source: For example, each pharyngeal neuron class is uniquely defined by characteristic signatures of neurotransmitter systems, from acetylcholine (ACh), glutamate (Glu) to serotonin, and by unique combinations of neuropeptide-encoding genes (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1E showing molecular markers for different pharyngeal neuron classes.

claim: Pharyngeal neurons are more similar to each other than to other neurons in the nervous system based on scRNA profiling.
source: While pharyngeal neurons are clearly different from one another, scRNA profiling has shown that their molecular signatures are more similar to each other than to other neurons in the nervous system (Taylor et al., 2021; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Taylor et al., 2021) and reference to Figure 1D showing transcriptome similarity.

claim: The C. elegans pharynx is essentially a single monolayer of cells organized into a tubular structure.
source: The organization of the C. elegans pharynx reveals some striking parallels to such a presumptive primitive nervous system: It is also essentially a single monolayer of cells that is organized into a tubular structure and the vast majority of constituent cells are myoepithelial cells (pharyngeal muscle) and polymodal, interconnected sensory/motor neurons (Cook et al., 2020; Mango, 2007; Portereiko and Mango, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the organization of the C. elegans pharynx.

claim: The vast majority of constituent cells in the C. elegans pharynx are myoepithelial cells (pharyngeal muscle) and polymodal, interconnected sensory/motor neurons.
source: The organization of the C. elegans pharynx reveals some striking parallels to such a presumptive primitive nervous system: It is also essentially a single monolayer of cells that is organized into a tubular structure and the vast majority of constituent cells are myoepithelial cells (pharyngeal muscle) and polymodal, interconnected sensory/motor neurons (Cook et al., 2020; Mango, 2007; Portereiko and Mango, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the cellular composition of the C. elegans pharynx.

claim: Pharyngeal neurons are not localized to ganglia but rather diffusely localized, resembling the architecture of more ancient nerve nets.
source: Pharyngeal neurons combine sensory, inter- and motor neuron features and are also not localized to ganglia but rather diffusely localized, resembling the architecture of more ancient nerve nets (Albertson and Thomson, 1976; Watanabe et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the organization of pharyngeal neurons.

claim: The interconnectivity of pharyngeal neurons displays less selectivity than non-pharyngeal neurons, such that mere physical proximity is an almost sufficient criterion for connectivity.
source: The interconnectivity of pharyngeal neurons also displays less selectivity than non-pharyngeal neurons, such that mere physical proximity is an almost sufficient criterion for connectivity (Cook et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Cook et al., 2020) describing the connectivity patterns of pharyngeal neurons.

claim: Some pharyngeal muscle and neurons derive from a common mother cell.
source: Moreover, pharyngeal neurons are closely related to non-neuronal pharyngeal cells by lineage; for example, some muscle and neurons derive from a common mother cell (Sulston et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sulston et al., 1983) describing the lineage relationships of pharyngeal cells.

claim: C. elegans contains several homologs of the Sine oculis/Six family of homeodomain proteins.
source: Genome sequence mining revealed several C. elegans homologs of the Sine oculis/Six family of homeodomain proteins (Ruvkun and Hobert, 1998) whose founding member was first identified in Drosophila for its role in eye patterning (Cheyette et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the identification of Sine oculis/Six family members in C. elegans.

claim: The Sine oculis/Six family of homeodomain proteins is characterized by the presence of a conserved domain, the ~150 amino acid-long SIX domain, located N-terminally to the DNA binding homeodomain.
source: This specific homeodomain transcription factor family is characterized by the presence of a conserved domain, located N-terminally to the DNA binding homeodomain, the ~150 amino acid-long SIX domain, involved in both protein-DNA, as well as protein-protein interactions (Kumar, 2009; Patrick et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the structural features of the SIX domain.

claim: C. elegans Six-type homeodomain proteins fall into several phylogenetically conserved families: the Sine oculis/Six1/2, the Six4/5, and the Six3/6 subfamily.
source: C. elegans Six-type homeodomain proteins fall into several, phylogenetically conserved families, the Sine oculis/Six1/2, the Six4/5, and the Six3/6 subfamily (Dozier et al., 2001; Kumar, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the phylogenetic classification of Six-type homeodomain proteins.

claim: Nematodes generally contain a single ortholog of the Sine oculis/Six1/2 subfamily of SIX homeodomain proteins.
source: Through the analysis of multiple nematode genome sequences, we found that nematodes generally contain a single ortholog of the Sine oculis/Six1/2 subfamily of SIX homeodomain proteins, but that this locus has duplicated in the Caenorhabditis genus into two immediately adjacent paralogs, ceh-33 and ceh-34 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from analysis of multiple nematode genome sequences and reference to Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Sine oculis/Six1/2 locus has duplicated in the Caenorhabditis genus into two immediately adjacent paralogs, ceh-33 and ceh-34.
source: Through the analysis of multiple nematode genome sequences, we found that nematodes generally contain a single ortholog of the Sine oculis/Six1/2 subfamily of SIX homeodomain proteins, but that this locus has duplicated in the Caenorhabditis genus into two immediately adjacent paralogs, ceh-33 and ceh-34 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from analysis of multiple nematode genome sequences and reference to Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CEH-33 protein shows no expression in the nervous system within or outside the pharynx at any developmental stage.
source: Using a fosmid-based reporter in which the ceh-33 locus is tagged with gfp, we found that the CEH-33 protein shows no expression in the nervous system within or outside the pharynx at any developmental stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a fosmid-based reporter showing CEH-33 expression pattern.

claim: CEH-33 is expressed in a subset of head muscle cells.
source: The only observed expression was in a subset of head muscle cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ceh-34 is expressed in all pharyngeal neurons but no other neurons.
source: A previously described reporter construct that contains the coding region and 3.8 kb of promoter region of the neighboring ceh-34 gene showed expression in all pharyngeal neurons (Hirose et al., 2010). A fosmid-based reporter shows the same expression pattern (Reilly et al., 2020). To further confirm this strikingly selective pattern of neuronal expression and also to examine expression at different developmental stages with the best possible reagent, we used the CRISPR/Cas9 system to engineer a reporter allele of ceh-34. This reporter shows the same expression as the fosmid-based reporter in all pharyngeal neurons, but no other neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple reporter constructs including a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered reporter allele, and citations to published literature (Hirose et al., 2010; Reilly et al., 2020).

claim: ceh-34 is turned on in the embryo at around the time of birth of pharyngeal neurons and is maintained in all pharyngeal neurons throughout all larval and adult stages.
source: The ceh-34 reporter is turned on in the embryo at around the time of birth of pharyngeal neurons and is maintained in all pharyngeal neurons throughout all larval and adult stages (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the ceh-34 reporter shown in Figure 2B.

claim: pha-4 is required for ceh-34 expression.
source: Crossing a ceh-34 reporter into pha-4(q490) mutant animals, we indeed observed a loss of ceh-34 expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from crossing experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ceh-34 does not affect pha-4 expression.
source: Conversely, ceh-34 does not affect pha-4 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: pha-4 is continuously expressed throughout the entire pharyngeal nervous system at all postembryonic stages.
source: We furthermore note that a pha-4 reporter allele that we generated through CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering is continuously expressed throughout the entire pharyngeal nervous system, at all postembryonic stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), raising the possibility that pha-4 may not only initiate, but also maintain ceh-34 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered pha-4 reporter allele shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ceh-34 null mutants (ot1014 and tm3733) result in a completely penetrant early larval arrest phenotype.
source: Both the ot1014 and tm3733 alleles result in a completely penetrant early larval arrest phenotype, as expected from loss of pharynx function and resulting inability to feed.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from phenotypic analysis of ceh-34 null mutants.

claim: ceh-34 is not required for the generation of pharyngeal neurons.
source: Using a pha-4 reporter that labels all pharyngeal cells, we observed no obvious differences in the number of pharyngeal cells in ceh-34 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The expression of pan-neuronal genes ric-4/SNAP25, ric-19/ICA1, rab-3/RAB3, and unc-11/AP180 is unaffected in ceh-34 mutants.
source: Moreover, the expression of the pan-neuronal genes ric-4/SNAP25, ric-19/ICA1, rab-3/RAB3, and unc-11/AP180 is unaffected (Figure 3A), indicating that pharyngeal neurons are generated and properly execute a generic neuronal differentiation program.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Seven of the 14 pharyngeal neuron classes use ACh as neurotransmitter.
source: We first considered the three classic neurotransmitters ACh, Glu, and serotonin which are employed in C. elegans much like in the enteric nervous system of other species: 7 of the 14 pharyngeal neuron classes use ACh as neurotransmitter, 4 use Glu, and 1 uses serotonin (NSM) (Horvitz et al., 1982; Pereira et al., 2015; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing neurotransmitter usage in pharyngeal neurons.

claim: Four of the 14 pharyngeal neuron classes use Glu as neurotransmitter.
source: We first considered the three classic neurotransmitters ACh, Glu, and serotonin which are employed in C. elegans much like in the enteric nervous system of other species: 7 of the 14 pharyngeal neuron classes use ACh as neurotransmitter, 4 use Glu, and 1 uses serotonin (NSM) (Horvitz et al., 1982; Pereira et al., 2015; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing neurotransmitter usage in pharyngeal neurons.

claim: One of the 14 pharyngeal neuron classes (NSM) uses serotonin as neurotransmitter.
source: We first considered the three classic neurotransmitters ACh, Glu, and serotonin which are employed in C. elegans much like in the enteric nervous system of other species: 7 of the 14 pharyngeal neuron classes use ACh as neurotransmitter, 4 use Glu, and 1 uses serotonin (NSM) (Horvitz et al., 1982; Pereira et al., 2015; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing neurotransmitter usage in pharyngeal neurons.

claim: The seven cholinergic, four glutamatergic, and single serotonergic pharyngeal neuron classes fail to acquire their respective neurotransmitter identity in ceh-34 mutants.
source: We examined the expression of all these markers, using various reporter genes, in all pharyngeal neurons of ceh-34 mutant animals and found that the seven cholinergic, four glutamatergic, and single serotonergic neuron classes fail to acquire their respective neurotransmitter identity (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The expression of the serotonin receptor ser-7 is strongly affected in different pharyngeal neuron types in ceh-34 mutants.
source: Using a combination of reporter transgenes and CRISPR/Cas9-engineered gfp reporter alleles, we found that the expression of mgl-1, glr-2, and ser-7 is strongly affected in different pharyngeal neuron types, if not entirely abrogated upon removal of ceh-34 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The expression of the metabotropic glutamate receptor mgl-1 is strongly affected in different pharyngeal neuron types in ceh-34 mutants.
source: Using a combination of reporter transgenes and CRISPR/Cas9-engineered gfp reporter alleles, we found that the expression of mgl-1, glr-2, and ser-7 is strongly affected in different pharyngeal neuron types, if not entirely abrogated upon removal of ceh-34 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The expression of the ionotropic glutamate receptor glr-2 is strongly affected in different pharyngeal neuron types in ceh-34 mutants.
source: Using a combination of reporter transgenes and CRISPR/Cas9-engineered gfp reporter alleles, we found that the expression of mgl-1, glr-2, and ser-7 is strongly affected in different pharyngeal neuron types, if not entirely abrogated upon removal of ceh-34 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Each pharyngeal neuron expresses a unique combination of neuropeptides and their receptor proteins.
source: In fact, each pharyngeal neuron expresses a unique combination of neuropeptides and their receptor proteins (Taylor et al., 2021; Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Taylor et al., 2021) and reference to Figure 5.

claim: trh-1 is expressed in the MI, M4, and M5 neurons.
source: C. elegans homologs of either the thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH-1) or its receptor (TRHR-1) are expressed in the pharyngeal nervous system (Hunt-Newbury et al., 2007; Van Sinay et al., 2017), a notion we confirmed and extended with CRISPR/Cas9-engineered reporter alleles, showing that trh-1 is expressed in the MI, M4, and M5 neurons and trhr-1 in the M1, M2, M3, and I5 neurons (Figure 4 and Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from CRISPR/Cas9-engineered reporter alleles shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5, and citations to published literature.

claim: trhr-1 is expressed in the M1, M2, M3, and I5 neurons.
source: C. elegans homologs of either the thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH-1) or its receptor (TRHR-1) are expressed in the pharyngeal nervous system (Hunt-Newbury et al., 2007; Van Sinay et al., 2017), a notion we confirmed and extended with CRISPR/Cas9-engineered reporter alleles, showing that trh-1 is expressed in the MI, M4, and M5 neurons and trhr-1 in the M1, M2, M3, and I5 neurons (Figure 4 and Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from CRISPR/Cas9-engineered reporter alleles shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5, and citations to published literature.

claim: The expression of trh-1 and trhr-1 reporter alleles in pharyngeal neurons is strongly affected in ceh-34 mutants.
source: We found that the expression of the trh-1 and trhr-1 reporter alleles in these pharyngeal neurons is strongly affected in ceh-34 mutants (Figure 4 and Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5A.

claim: The expression of nine neuropeptides (flp-2, flp-4, flp-5, flp-15, flp-21, flp-28, nlp-3, nlp-8, nlp-13) is affected in ceh-34 mutants.
source: We found that the expression of all of these nine neuropeptides, analyzed with either reporter transgenes or CRISPR/Cas9 genome-engineered gfp reporter alleles, is affected in ceh-34 mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: gur-3 is expressed in two pharyngeal neuron classes and its expression is lost in ceh-34 mutants.
source: A gustatory receptor family member, gur-3, a possible light receptor (Bhatla and Horvitz, 2015), is expressed in two pharyngeal neuron classes and its expression is lost in ceh-34 mutants (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and a citation to published literature (Bhatla and Horvitz, 2015).

claim: glr-7 is expressed in six pharyngeal neuron classes (I2, I3, I6, M2, M3, and NSM).
source: We examined expression of glr-7 expression, normally observed in six pharyngeal neuron classes (I2, I3, I6, M2, M3, and NSM), in ceh-34 mutants and found its expression to be completely lost (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: glr-7 expression is completely lost in ceh-34 mutants.
source: We examined expression of glr-7 expression, normally observed in six pharyngeal neuron classes (I2, I3, I6, M2, M3, and NSM), in ceh-34 mutants and found its expression to be completely lost (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ceh-34 is required for proper str-97 expression.
source: Finally, we analyzed the expression of str-97, a putative chemosensory receptor of the GPCR family which we found to be expressed in several pharyngeal neurons (Vidal et al., 2018; Figure 6A). We found that ceh-34 is required for proper str-97 expression (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and a citation to published literature (Vidal et al., 2018).

claim: Pharyngeal neurons express the hormone FLR-2, homologous to glycoprotein hormone alpha subunit, that signals to the intestine to orchestrate antimicrobial defense.
source: For example, pharyngeal neurons express a hormone, FLR-2, homologous to glycoprotein hormone alpha subunit, that signals to the intestine to orchestrate antimicrobial defense (Oishi et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Oishi et al., 2009).

claim: Pharyngeal neurons secrete pore-forming polypeptides that directly kill bacteria, such as the SPP-12 protein.
source: Pharyngeal neurons also secrete pore-forming polypeptides that directly kill bacteria, such as the SPP-12 protein (Hoeckendorf et al., 2012), as well as a defensin-type antimicrobial peptide, ABF-2 and fungal-induced peptides (FIPR proteins; Kato et al., 2002; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hoeckendorf et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2002; Taylor et al., 2021).

claim: The spp-12 reporter is expressed in I4 and M4 neurons.
source: We found that the spp-12 reporter is expressed in I4 and M4 neurons, the flr-2::SL2::gfp::h2b reporter allele is expressed in five pharyngeal neuron classes (I4, I5, M1, M4, and M5), and the htrl-1::SL2::gfp::h2b reporter allele is expressed in all pharyngeal neurons (and in all other pharyngeal cells, but nowhere outside the pharynx at the L1 stage; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The flr-2::SL2::gfp::h2b reporter allele is expressed in five pharyngeal neuron classes (I4, I5, M1, M4, and M5).
source: We found that the spp-12 reporter is expressed in I4 and M4 neurons, the flr-2::SL2::gfp::h2b reporter allele is expressed in five pharyngeal neuron classes (I4, I5, M1, M4, and M5), and the htrl-1::SL2::gfp::h2b reporter allele is expressed in all pharyngeal neurons (and in all other pharyngeal cells, but nowhere outside the pharynx at the L1 stage; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The htrl-1::SL2::gfp::h2b reporter allele is expressed in all pharyngeal neurons and in all other pharyngeal cells, but nowhere outside the pharynx at the L1 stage.
source: We found that the spp-12 reporter is expressed in I4 and M4 neurons, the flr-2::SL2::gfp::h2b reporter allele is expressed in five pharyngeal neuron classes (I4, I5, M1, M4, and M5), and the htrl-1::SL2::gfp::h2b reporter allele is expressed in all pharyngeal neurons (and in all other pharyngeal cells, but nowhere outside the pharynx at the L1 stage; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The flr-2 reporter allele is expressed in the AVL and DVB neurons, the only extrapharyngeal neurons of the C. elegans nervous system that innervate gut tissue.
source: A notable feature of the extrapharyngeal expression of the flr-2 reporter allele is expression in the AVL and DVB neurons (Figure 6B), the only extrapharyngeal neurons of the C. elegans nervous system that innervate gut tissue (not the foregut, but the midgut; White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and a citation to published literature (White et al., 1986).

claim: Expression of spp-12, flr-2, and htrl-1 is severely reduced or eliminated in pharyngeal neurons in ceh-34 mutants.
source: Crossing these reporters into a ceh-34 mutant background, we found that expression of all three genes (spp-12, flr-2, htrl-1) is severely reduced or eliminated in pharyngeal neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: kin-36 displays pan-pharyngeal neuron expression and is also expressed in all other pharyngeal cell types, but no cell types outside the pharynx, except some unidentified vulval cells.
source: To confirm this expression pattern, we tagged the kin-36 locus with a gfp::H2B::SL2 cassette at its 5' end, using CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering. We found that kin-36 indeed displays pan-pharyngeal neuron expression; expression is also observed in all other pharyngeal cell types, but no cell types outside the pharynx, except some unidentified vulval cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered reporter allele shown in Figure 6C.

claim: kin-36 expression appears to be selectively lost from many, albeit not all pharyngeal neurons in ceh-34 mutants.
source: Crossing the kin-36 reporter allele into ceh-34 mutants, we observed what appears to be selective loss of kin-36 expression from many, albeit not all pharyngeal neurons, a similar effect to what we observed for htrl-1 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: ceh-34 is required for the adoption of a broad palette of individual molecular features of all pharyngeal neurons.
source: We conclude that ceh-34 is required for the adoption of a broad palette of individual molecular features of all pharyngeal neurons, consistent with a role as a terminal selector of neuronal identity of all pharyngeal neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cumulative data presented in the manuscript showing effects of ceh-34 on multiple molecular markers.

claim: ceh-34 only affects neuron type-specific features, but not features that are expressed by all neurons throughout the nervous system.
source: Like other terminal selectors, ceh-34 only affects neuron type-specific features, but not features that are expressed by all neurons throughout the nervous system.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data showing that pan-neuronal markers are unaffected in ceh-34 mutants while neuron type-specific markers are affected.

claim: Postembryonic 5-Ph-IAA addition at either larval or adult stages resulted in downregulation of four tested markers for the differentiated state of different pharyngeal neuron classes: eat-4/VGluT, unc-17/VAChT, ser-7, and spp-12.
source: Postembryonic 5-Ph-IAA addition at either larval or adult stages resulted in downregulation of four tested markers for the differentiated state of different pharyngeal neuron classes, eat-4/VGluT, unc-17/VAChT, ser-7, and spp-12 (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from temporally controlled protein depletion experiments shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Postembryonic CEH-34 depletion at either larval or adult stages results in substantial defects in pharyngeal pumping.
source: Using again the AID approach, we found that postembryonic CEH-34 depletion at either larval or adult stages results in substantial defects in pharyngeal pumping, as expected from a disruption of enteric nervous system function (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from temporally controlled protein depletion experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ceh-34 is required to maintain differentiated features of pharyngeal neurons.
source: We conclude that ceh-34 is required to maintain differentiated features of pharyngeal neurons and therefore fulfills another key criterion to classify as a terminal selector of pharyngeal neuron identity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data from temporally controlled protein depletion experiments.

claim: Although their identity is not properly specified in ceh-34 mutants, pharyngeal neurons retain the capability to grow neuronal projections; however, axonal tracts are severely disorganized.
source: This ceh-34 promoter transgene (otIs762) reveals that although their identity is not properly specified, as described above, pharyngeal neurons retain the capability to grow neuronal projections in ceh-34 mutants; however, axonal tracts are severely disorganized (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: ceh-34 null mutants show a severe disorganization of presynaptic clusters throughout the entire pharyngeal nervous system.
source: In ceh-34 null mutants, we observed not only a disruption of axonal tract anatomy, but a severe disorganization of presynaptic clusters throughout the entire pharyngeal nervous system (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Postembryonic CEH-34 depletion throughout larval stages or in the adult stage results in synaptic clusters becoming disorganized, such that ectopic presynaptic clusters form at ectopic locations in the isthmus of the pharynx.
source: To this end, we again made use of the AID system and removed CEH-34::mNG::AID either throughout larval stages or in the adult stage. In both cases, we found that such depletion resulted in synaptic clusters becoming disorganized, such that ectopic presynaptic clusters form at ectopic locations in the isthmus of the pharynx (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from temporally controlled protein depletion experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In ceh-34(n4796) animals, specific axon branches fail to form in NSM and I5 neuron types.
source: Focusing on two neuron types, NSM and I5, we found that in both types, specific axons branches fail to form in ceh-34(n4796) animals (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: ceh-34 is required to establish and maintain proper pharyngeal nervous system architecture.
source: We conclude that ceh-34 is required to establish and maintain proper pharyngeal nervous system architecture.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cumulative data showing effects of ceh-34 on axonal projections and synaptic organization.

claim: The SLT-1 axon guidance cue is required for proper axon guidance in M2 and NSM neuron classes.
source: A genetic analysis of axon guidance and circuit formation has only been conducted in a small number of pharyngeal neurons, mainly the M2 and NSM neuron classes (Pilon, 2008). In both neuron classes, the SLT-1 axon guidance cue, the C. elegans ortholog of Slit, has been found to be required for proper axon guidance (Axäng et al., 2008; Rauthan et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Axäng et al., 2008; Rauthan et al., 2007).

claim: Other pharyngeal neurons also display axon pathfinding defects in slt-1 mutants.
source: We extended this phenotypic characterization, finding that other pharyngeal neurons also display axon pathfinding defects in slt-1 mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: slt-1 is selectively expressed in seven pharyngeal neuron classes (I2, I6, M1, M2, M4, M5, and MI) at the first larval stage.
source: To examine potential links between slt-1 and ceh-34, we made use of a promoter::gfp fusion that captures the entire upstream intergenic region of the slt-1 locus (Hao et al., 2001) and which shows selective expression in seven pharyngeal neuron classes (I2, I6, M1, M2, M4, M5, and MI) at the first larval stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a promoter::gfp fusion and a citation to published literature (Hao et al., 2001).

claim: slt-1 expression is strongly affected in ceh-34 mutants.
source: We found that slt-1 expression is strongly affected in ceh-34 mutants (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: rig-3 and rig-6 have been implicated in axon outgrowth and synapse function in the C. elegans nervous system.
source: Two Ig superfamily members, rig-3 and rig-6 (the sole C. elegans ortholog of contactin), have previously been implicated in axon outgrowth and synapse function in the C. elegans nervous system (Babu et al., 2011; Bhardwaj et al., 2020; Katidou et al., 2013; Kim and Emmons, 2017) and promoter fusion transgenes have indicated their expression in pharyngeal neurons (Schwarz et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Babu et al., 2011; Bhardwaj et al., 2020; Katidou et al., 2013; Kim and Emmons, 2017; Schwarz et al., 2009).

claim: rig-3 and rig-6 are broadly expressed in many pharyngeal neurons.
source: We used CRISPR/Cas9 to tag both loci with gfp and found that both genes are broadly expressed in many pharyngeal neurons (Figures 1E and 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from CRISPR/Cas9-engineered reporter alleles shown in Figures 1E and 8E.

claim: ceh-34 affects the pharyngeal neuron expression of both rig-3 and rig-6 reporter alleles.
source: ceh-34 affects the pharyngeal neuron expression of both rig-3 and rig-6 reporter alleles (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The C. elegans ortholog of Eyes absent, called eya-1, directly physically interacts with CEH-34 protein.
source: The C. elegans ortholog of Eyes absent, called eya-1 (Furuya et al., 2005), also directly physically interacts with CEH-34 protein (Amin et al., 2009; Hirose et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Amin et al., 2009; Hirose et al., 2010).

claim: eya-1 is expressed in all pharyngeal neurons throughout all larval and adult stages.
source: We first examined eya-1 expression in pharyngeal neurons using a genomic fragment that contains the entire, gfp-tagged eya-1 locus (Furuya et al., 2005). We observed expression in all pharyngeal neurons throughout all larval and adult stages, a phenocopy of the ceh-34 expression pattern (Figure 9A), that is also corroborated by our recent scRNA analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a gfp-tagged eya-1 locus shown in Figure 9A and citations to published literature (Furuya et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2021).

claim: eya-1 expression requires ceh-34 function.
source: Moreover, we found that eya-1 expression requires ceh-34 function, suggesting that ceh-34 acts in a feedforward configuration to induce its own transcriptional cofactor (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Animals carrying the eya-1(ok654) deletion allele display pharyngeal neuron specification defects, albeit much milder than those observed in ceh-34 null mutant animals.
source: Animals that carry a deletion of a part of the eya-1 locus, ok654, display pharyngeal neuron specification defects, albeit much milder than those observed in ceh-34 null mutant animals (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The larval arrest phenotype of ceh-34 null mutants is more penetrant than that of eya-1 mutants, which are very slow growing, but still homozygous viable.
source: The larval arrest phenotype of ceh-34 null mutants is also more penetrant than that of eya-1 mutants, which are very slow growing, but still homozygous viable (Furuya et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from phenotypic analysis and a citation to published literature (Furuya et al., 2005).

claim: Animals carrying the eya-1(ot1197) null allele display phenotypes that are indistinguishable from those of eya-1(ok654) animals.
source: To exclude the possibility that the ok654 allele is not a null allele, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to generate a null allele in which the entire locus is deleted. Animals carrying this deletion allele (ot1197) display phenotypes that are indistinguishable from those of ok654 animals. They are still homozygous viable, albeit as slowly growing as ok654 animals, and they display very similar, limited neuronal cell fate marker defects (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a CRISPR/Cas9-generated null allele shown in Figure 9C.

claim: ceh-34 may be able to partly function without eya-1.
source: Given the milder spectrum of eya-1 defects compared to ceh-34 null mutants, we conclude that ceh-34 may be able to partly function without eya-1.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of phenotypes between eya-1 and ceh-34 mutants.

claim: The sole C. elegans ortholog of Dachshund is not expressed in pharyngeal neurons.
source: However, the sole C. elegans ortholog of Dachshund is not expressed in pharyngeal neurons (Colosimo et al., 2004; Taylor et al., 2021) and dac-1 null mutants also do not display the larval growth/arrest phenotype characteristic of ceh-34 and eya-1 mutants (Colosimo et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Colosimo et al., 2004; Taylor et al., 2021).

claim: dac-1 null mutants do not display the larval growth/arrest phenotype characteristic of ceh-34 and eya-1 mutants.
source: However, the sole C. elegans ortholog of Dachshund is not expressed in pharyngeal neurons (Colosimo et al., 2004; Taylor et al., 2021) and dac-1 null mutants also do not display the larval growth/arrest phenotype characteristic of ceh-34 and eya-1 mutants (Colosimo et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Colosimo et al., 2004).

claim: Each individual pharyngeal neuron expresses a unique combination of homeobox genes, in addition to pan-pharyngeal ceh-34.
source: As candidates for such cofactors, we considered homeobox genes, for two reasons: (1) like any other neuron in the C. elegans nervous system, each individual pharyngeal neuron expresses a unique combination of homeobox genes, in addition to pan-pharyngeal ceh-34 (Reilly et al., 2020);
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Reilly et al., 2020).

claim: The homeobox gene ceh-2 is required for proper function of the M3 neuron.
source: For example, the homeobox gene ceh-2, the C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate EMX and Drosophila Ems, is required for proper function of the M3 neuron, but effects of ceh-2 on molecular aspects of M3 neuron differentiation had not been reported (Aspöck et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Aspöck et al., 2003).

claim: The ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele displays only subtle if any marker expression effects on its own in NSM neurons.
source: Unlike the ceh-34 null allele, which results in very strong expression defects of all NSM molecular markers (Figures 3—6), the n4796 allele displays only subtle if any marker expression effects on its own (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: A combination of the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele with the unc-86(n846) mutation results in strong synergistic differentiation defects of NSM.
source: However, when combined with a mutant allele of unc-86, a POU homeobox gene that affects many but not all NSM marker genes (Zhang et al., 2014), strong synergistic differentiation defects of NSM are observed (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10A and a citation to published literature (Zhang et al., 2014).

claim: Cholinergic identity of I1 neurons is not affected in unc-86(n846) single mutants.
source: While cholinergic identity, visualized via unc-17/VAChT expression, is not affected in unc-86(n846) single mutants, a combination of the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele with the unc-86(n846) mutation results in I1 losing its cholinergic identity (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: A combination of the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele with the unc-86(n846) mutation results in I1 losing its cholinergic identity.
source: While cholinergic identity, visualized via unc-17/VAChT expression, is not affected in unc-86(n846) single mutants, a combination of the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele with the unc-86(n846) mutation results in I1 losing its cholinergic identity (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The I2 neuron expresses the LIM homeobox gene ceh-14, the C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate Lhx3/4.
source: Synergistic interactions are also observed in the glutamatergic I2 neuron pair. Like the I1 neurons, no identity regulators were previously known for this neuron class. Our homeobox gene expression atlas (Reilly et al., 2020) showed that the I2 neuron expresses the LIM homeobox gene ceh-14, the C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate Lhx3/4.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Reilly et al., 2020).

claim: No other pharyngeal neuron expresses ceh-14.
source: Our homeobox gene expression atlas (Reilly et al., 2020) showed that the I2 neuron expresses the LIM homeobox gene ceh-14, the C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate Lhx3/4. No other pharyngeal neuron expresses ceh-14.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the homeobox gene expression atlas (Reilly et al., 2020).

claim: ceh-14 single null mutants show no effect on eat-4/VGluT expression in I2 neurons.
source: While ceh-14 single null mutants show no effect on eat-4/VGluT expression (the marker of glutamatergic identity), in combination with the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele, a strong synergistic effect on glutamatergic identity acquisition is observed in I2 (Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: In combination with the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele, a strong synergistic effect on glutamatergic identity acquisition is observed in I2 neurons.
source: While ceh-14 single null mutants show no effect on eat-4/VGluT expression (the marker of glutamatergic identity), in combination with the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele, a strong synergistic effect on glutamatergic identity acquisition is observed in I2 (Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The neuropeptide nlp-8 is synergistically regulated by ceh-34 and ceh-14 in I2 neurons.
source: Another molecular marker for I2 identity, the neuropeptide nlp-8, is also synergistically regulated by ceh-34 and ceh-14 (Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The I3 neuron expresses ceh-2 and pros-1.
source: The previously unstudied cholinergic I3 neuron class expresses, in addition to ceh-34, the C. elegans ortholog of Empty spiracles/EMX, ceh-2 (Aspöck et al., 2003; Reilly et al., 2020), as well as the Prospero ortholog pros-1, whose function in the nervous system has not previously been examined.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Aspöck et al., 2003; Reilly et al., 2020).

claim: In pros-1 null mutant animals, cholinergic identity of I3 is not properly acquired.
source: We find that in pros-1 null mutant animals, cholinergic identity of I3, measured with an unc-17/VAChT reporter transgene, is not properly acquired (Figure 10D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The ceh-2(ch4) null allele alone shows a reduction of unc-17/VAChT expression in I3 neurons.
source: The ceh-2(ch4) null allele alone also shows a reduction of unc-17/VAChT expression (Figure 10F), as well as a reduction of the serotonin receptor ser-7 expression (Figure 10E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: The ceh-2(ch4) null allele alone shows a reduction of ser-7 expression in I3 neurons.
source: The ceh-2(ch4) null allele alone also shows a reduction of unc-17/VAChT expression (Figure 10F), as well as a reduction of the serotonin receptor ser-7 expression (Figure 10E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: In combination with the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele, unc-17/VAChT expression, and, hence, cholinergic identity of I3, is eliminated in ceh-2 mutant animals.
source: In combination with the ceh-34(n4796) hypomorphic allele, unc-17/VAChT expression, and, hence, cholinergic identity of I3, is eliminated in ceh-2 mutant animals (Figure 10F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: ceh-2 is expressed in the glutamatergic M3 neurons.
source: Apart from expression in I3, the EMX ortholog ceh-2 is also expressed in the glutamatergic M3 neurons and is required for proper M3 function (Aspöck et al., 2003), but molecular correlates for this functional defect have not previously been identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Aspöck et al., 2003).

claim: In ceh-2 single mutants, expression of the eat-4/VGluT identity marker is affected in M3 neurons.
source: We found that in ceh-2 single mutants, expression of the eat-4/VGluT identity marker is affected in M3 (Figure 11A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The M5 neuron expresses the Msh/Msx ortholog vab-15.
source: The cholinergic M5 neuron expresses, in addition to ceh-34, the Msh/Msx ortholog vab-15 (Reilly et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Reilly et al., 2020).

claim: vab-15(ot1136) null mutant animals are very slow growing, but still homozygous viable.
source: Since only a hypomorphic allele of vab-15 was previously available (Du and Chalfie, 2001), we generated a molecular null allele, ot1136, through CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering (Figure 11—figure supplement 1A). In contrast to the hypomorphic allele, these null mutant animals are very slow growing, but still homozygous viable.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a CRISPR/Cas9-generated null allele.

claim: In vab-15(ot1136) animals, there is a complete loss of expression of the cholinergic marker unc-17/VAChT and the neuropeptidergic marker trh-1 in M5 neurons.
source: We found a complete loss of expression of the cholinergic marker unc-17/VAChT, as well as the neuropeptidergic marker, trh-1, in vab-15(ot1136) animals (Figure 11B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: The glutamatergic MI neuron expresses the sole worm ortholog of the Goosecoid homeobox gene, ceh-45.
source: In our previous genome-wide analysis of homeobox gene expression (Reilly et al., 2020), we had shown that the glutamatergic MI neuron expresses the sole worm ortholog of the Goosecoid homeobox gene, ceh-45.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Reilly et al., 2020).

claim: ceh-45 is expressed in the MI and I1 neurons.
source: Embryonically, ceh-45 is expressed in multiple pharyngeal tissues (Ma et al., 2021), but its expression resolves to exclusive expression in the MI and I1 neurons (Reilly et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ma et al., 2021; Reilly et al., 2020).

claim: ceh-45 null mutant animals display partially penetrant embryonic lethality, with escapers being slow growing.
source: We examined ceh-45 function by generating a null allele using CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering, ot1065 (Figure 11—figure supplement 1A). ceh-45 null mutant animals display partially penetrant embryonic lethality, with escapers being slow growing.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a CRISPR/Cas9-generated null allele.

claim: Glutamatergic identity specification of MI (as assessed by eat-4/VGluT expression) is strongly affected in surviving ceh-45 null mutant animals.
source: Mirroring the ceh-34 defects, we found that glutamatergic identity specification of MI (as assessed by eat-4/VGluT expression) is strongly affected in surviving ceh-45 null mutant animals (Figure 11C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Expression of the neuropeptide trh-1 is affected in MI neurons in ceh-45 null mutant animals.
source: Similarly, expression of the neuropeptide trh-1 is also affected in MI (Figure 11C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Nine phylogenetically conserved homeobox genes appear to collaborate with ceh-34 in 8 of the 14 pharyngeal neuron classes to specify their proper identity.
source: In conclusion, nine phylogenetically conserved homeobox genes appear to collaborate with ceh-34 in 8 of the 14 pharyngeal neuron classes to specify their proper identity (summarized in Figure 12).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 12.

claim: CEH-34 appears to act as a terminal selector of pharyngeal neuron identity.
source: We have shown here that a Sine oculis ortholog, ceh-34, orchestrates the terminal differentiation program of all pharyngeal neurons. CEH-34 appears to act as a terminal selector of pharyngeal neuron identity, as inferred from its requirement to initiate terminal neuronal differentiation programs in all pharyngeal neurons (without affecting pan-neuronal identity, a unifying trait of all terminal selectors), as well as its continuous role in maintaining the differentiated state (another defining trait of terminal selectors).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cumulative data presented in the manuscript showing effects of ceh-34 on terminal differentiation and maintenance.

claim: CEH-34 controls anatomical (axon outgrowth and synapse formation), molecular, and functional features of pharyngeal neurons.
source: The aspects of the differentiation program that we consider here, and found to be under control of ceh-34, include anatomical (axon outgrowth and synapse formation), molecular, and functional features.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CEH-34 likely controls diverse phenotypic identity features in a direct manner.
source: There is good reason to believe that CEH-34 controls these diverse phenotypic identity features in a direct manner, that is, it may not act through intermediary factors. CEH-34 is among the many C. elegans transcription factors whose binding sites have been determined in vitro through protein binding microarrays (Narasimhan et al., 2015) and a phylogenetic footprinting pipeline reveals that these motifs are significantly enriched in the single cell transcriptome of most pharyngeal neuron classes (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on data from protein binding microarrays and phylogenetic footprinting, supported by citations to published literature (Narasimhan et al., 2015; Glenwinkel et al., 2021).

claim: Based on extensive gene expression pattern analysis, including recent scRNA data, there is no other transcription factor that so selectively and comprehensively defines all pharyngeal, but no non-pharyngeal neuronal cell types.
source: Within the nervous system, the selectivity of ceh-34 expression in all pharyngeal neurons is remarkable – based on extensive gene expression pattern analysis, including recent scRNA data, there is no other transcription factor that so selectively and comprehensively defines all pharyngeal, but no non-pharyngeal neuronal cell types.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on extensive gene expression pattern analysis.

claim: pha-4 acts both as a pioneer factor and to induce the expression of a number of different terminal selectors for different tissue types within the foregut.
source: We found that the key determinant of this expression is the organ selector PHA-4 (Gaudet and Mango, 2002; Horner et al., 1998; Kalb et al., 1998; Mango et al., 1994), which is expressed earlier in development to act both as a pioneer factor (Hsu et al., 2015) and to induce the expression of a number of different terminal selectors for different tissue types within the foregut – the ceh-34 gene for all neurons (this paper), the bHLH transcription factor hlh-6 for pharyngeal gland cells (Smit et al., 2008) and the Nk-type homeobox gene ceh-22 for pharyngeal muscle identity (Vilimas et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gaudet and Mango, 2002; Horner et al., 1998; Kalb et al., 1998; Mango et al., 1994; Hsu et al., 2015; Smit et al., 2008; Vilimas et al., 2004).

claim: PHA-4 may act in a regulatory feedforward motif configuration, where it not only induces tissue-type terminal selectors (ceh-34, hlh-6, ceh-22), but then also collaborates with them to induce and maintain terminal differentiation batteries.
source: Given the continuous expression of PHA-4 throughout postembryonic life, it is conceivable that PHA-4 acts in a regulatory feedforward motif configuration, where it not only induces tissue-type terminal selectors (ceh-34, hlh-6, ceh-22), but then also collaborates with them to induce and maintain terminal differentiation batteries.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the continuous expression of PHA-4.

claim: CEH-34 is a shared component of neuron type-specific terminal selector complexes, such that CEH-34 interacts with a distinct set of at least eight homeodomain cofactors to impose unique features in distinct pharyngeal neuron types.
source: Our work indicates that CEH-34 is a shared component of neuron type-specific terminal selector complexes, such that CEH-34 interacts with a distinct set of at least eight homeodomain cofactors to impose unique features in distinct pharyngeal neuron types.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cumulative data presented in the manuscript showing genetic interactions between ceh-34 and other homeobox genes.

claim: The in vitro-determined binding sites for several homeodomain cofactors display a phylogenetically conserved enrichment in the respective neuron type-specific gene batteries.
source: As is the case for CEH-34 target sites, the in vitro-determined binding sites for several of these homeodomain cofactors display a phylogenetically conserved enrichment in the respective neuron type-specific gene batteries (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).

claim: CEH-34 and UNC-86 binding sites are co-enriched in the I1 neuronal transcriptome.
source: For example, CEH-34 and UNC-86 binding sites are co-enriched in the I1 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-14 binding sites in the I2 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-2 in the I3 transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-45 in the MI transcriptome, and VAB-15 and CEH-34 in the M5 transcriptome (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).

claim: CEH-34 and CEH-14 binding sites are co-enriched in the I2 neuronal transcriptome.
source: For example, CEH-34 and UNC-86 binding sites are co-enriched in the I1 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-14 binding sites in the I2 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-2 in the I3 transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-45 in the MI transcriptome, and VAB-15 and CEH-34 in the M5 transcriptome (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).

claim: CEH-34 and CEH-2 binding sites are co-enriched in the I3 transcriptome.
source: For example, CEH-34 and UNC-86 binding sites are co-enriched in the I1 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-14 binding sites in the I2 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-2 in the I3 transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-45 in the MI transcriptome, and VAB-15 and CEH-34 in the M5 transcriptome (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).

claim: CEH-34 and CEH-45 binding sites are co-enriched in the MI transcriptome.
source: For example, CEH-34 and UNC-86 binding sites are co-enriched in the I1 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-14 binding sites in the I2 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-2 in the I3 transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-45 in the MI transcriptome, and VAB-15 and CEH-34 in the M5 transcriptome (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).

claim: VAB-15 and CEH-34 binding sites are co-enriched in the M5 transcriptome.
source: For example, CEH-34 and UNC-86 binding sites are co-enriched in the I1 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-14 binding sites in the I2 neuronal transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-2 in the I3 transcriptome, CEH-34 and CEH-45 in the MI transcriptome, and VAB-15 and CEH-34 in the M5 transcriptome (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Glenwinkel et al., 2021).

claim: The findings reveal a common terminal selector-based regulatory logic for how a self-contained, enteric nervous system acquires its terminal differentiated state.
source: Taken together, our findings not only reveal a common terminal selector-based regulatory logic for how a self-contained, enteric nervous system acquires its terminal differentiated state.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cumulative data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In flies, the Sine oculis paralog Optix is expressed in the frontal ganglion, which constitutes the nervous system of insect foreguts.
source: Arguing for a conserved function of Six homeodomain factors in enteric nervous system differentiation is the observation that in flies, the Sine oculis paralog Optix is indeed expressed in the frontal ganglion (Seo et al., 1999), which constitutes the nervous system of insect foreguts (Hartenstein, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Seo et al., 1999; Hartenstein, 1997).

claim: The entire stomatogastric ganglion does not form in Sine oculis mutants in Drosophila.
source: In the context of studying Sine oculis function in the Drosophila corpus cardiacum, it was also noted that the entire stomatogastric ganglion, that is, the entire enteric nervous system (of which the frontal ganglion is a part) does not form in Sine oculis mutants (De Velasco et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (De Velasco et al., 2004).

claim: In sea urchin, pharyngeal neurons express, and require for their proper development, the Sine oculis paralog Six3.
source: In sea urchin, pharyngeal neurons also express, and require for their proper development, the Sine oculis paralog Six3 (Wei et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Wei et al., 2011).

claim: The paired-type homeobox gene Phox2b is expressed in enteric nervous system precursors and required early in development for the generation of all enteric ganglia in vertebrates.
source: Notably, another homeobox gene appears to have a critical and very broad function in vertebrate enteric nervous system development that is akin to the broadness of ceh-34 function in C. elegans. The paired-type homeobox gene Phox2b is expressed in enteric nervous system precursors and required early in development for the generation of all enteric ganglia (Pattyn et al., 1999; Tiveron et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pattyn et al., 1999; Tiveron et al., 1996).

claim: Phox2b is continuously expressed throughout the adult enteric nervous system in vertebrates.
source: While Phox2b is also continuously expressed throughout the adult enteric nervous system (Corpening et al., 2008; Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021), its function in terminal differentiation and perhaps even maintenance of enteric neurons identity remains to be examined, for example, via temporally controlled, postdevelopmental knock-out in juvenile or adult stage animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Corpening et al., 2008; Drokhlyansky et al., 2020; Morarach et al., 2021).

claim: Additional homeobox genes show highly selective expression patterns within the vertebrate enteric nervous system, effectively discriminating distinct neuronal subtypes.
source: Remarkably, additional homeobox genes have recently been noted to show highly selective expression patterns within the vertebrate enteric nervous system, effectively discriminating distinct neuronal subtypes (Memic et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Memic et al., 2018).

claim: The Meis ortholog Pbx3 plays an important role in the postmitotic specification of distinct enteric neuron types in vertebrates.
source: One of them, the Meis ortholog Pbx3, has been confirmed to play an important role in the postmitotic specification of distinct enteric neuron types (Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Morarach et al., 2021).

claim: The overall logic of a pan-enteric homeobox gene, cooperating with cell type-specific homeobox genes, may be conserved from worms to vertebrates.
source: Hence, it appears that the overall logic of a pan-enteric homeobox gene, cooperating with cell type-specific homeobox genes, may be conserved from worms to vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the comparison of findings in C. elegans and vertebrates.

claim: It has been proposed that enteric nervous systems preceded, and then paralleled the emergence of centralized nervous systems of bilaterian animals.
source: Based on a number of anatomical and functional features, it has been proposed that enteric nervous systems preceded, and then paralleled the emergence of centralized nervous systems of bilaterian animals (Furness and Stebbing, 2018; Gilbert, 2019; Klimovich and Bosch, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Furness and Stebbing, 2018; Gilbert, 2019; Klimovich and Bosch, 2018).

claim: If pharyngeal neurons indeed resemble a more primitive, ancestral state of neurons, CEH-34/Sine oculis may represent an ancestral determinant of neuronal cell types.
source: If pharyngeal neurons indeed resemble a more primitive, ancestral state of neurons, our observation that CEH-34 acts as a terminal selector in these neurons would point to the ancient nature of (1) a terminal selector-type logic of neuronal identity specification and (2) the deployment of a homeobox gene in such function. Sine oculis homologs appear to be employed broadly in sensory neuron specification across animal phylogeny, even in the most basal metazoan (Jacobs et al., 2007). CEH-34/Sine oculis may represent an ancestral determinant of neuronal cell types.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the features of pharyngeal neurons and the function of CEH-34, supported by a citation to published literature (Jacobs et al., 2007).
